hook_text: Two graphs, both made of bars. In one the bars stand apart. In the other they touch. Mixing them up is the most common graph mistake in Grade 9.
clip_script: Sixty learners: 33 walk, 21 take a taxi, 6 come by car. Draw a tower for each: a bar graph. The towers stand apart, with gaps, because walk and taxi are separate words; there is nothing in between. Now a different set of data: how far thirty learners live from school, grouped in bands, 0 to under 1 kilometre, 1 to under 2, 2 to under 3, and so on. Draw a bar over each band, and this time the bars TOUCH. Why? Because the bands run into each other on a number line. There is no gap between 0.99 kilometres and 1 kilometre. Touching bars make a histogram, and the touching is the point: it says the data is one continuous stretch of numbers, not a list of separate categories. Words apart, numbers together. And a pie chart? Only for shares of a whole, and only after you have worked out the angles: 33 out of 60 is 198 degrees. Say it: words apart, numbers touch.
visual_style: Three separate towers labelled walk, taxi, car with clear gaps; then a number line from 0 to 5 with five bars sliding shoulder to shoulder; a red gap appears between two histogram bars and is struck through; a pie slice of 198 degrees sweeps open with a protractor.
pacing: Bar graph fast, the histogram slow with the bars sliding together, the reason at speaking pace, the pie as a quick coda.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for choosing your own intervals, broken-line graphs, scatter plots and the error museum.
